rv.q: This is a Rolls Royce of a revival, precision-tooled and carrying the weight of the show’s history lightly.
But even that isn't enough to distract from the spectacle of My Fair Lady, a hypnotic show that keeps you in Eliza's captivating world with an unmissable performance.
This Bartlett Sher production is unashamedly sensuous.
This is the “Ascot Gavotte”, one of the highlights of Bartlett Sher’s spry, enjoyable Theater staging of Lerner and Loewe’s beloved musical My Fair Lady.
This is a very decent, very stylish, eventually quite audacious My Fair Lady.
Bartlett Sher’s timid production, first seen in New York four years ago, will make them merely smile and shuffle.
And while there’s plenty to recommend it, there are elements of this production that feel underpowered.
This production will just about satisfy its fans, without offering enough to win over sceptics.
Almost everything else, unfortunately, is problematic.
This is a thoughtful grappling with a rich and complex musical, balancing old-fashioned charm with fresh ideas, and, at its best, blossoming into a truly loverly night out.
Nevertheless, it is all part of the theatricality that drives this production of what must be the most English of American musicals.
She shimmers like sunshine as she sings to the dawn in "I Could All Night", and grounds the whole three-hour show with a faultless depiction of someone simply wanting to get ahead in the world.
That doesn’t stop this one from being a decent night out.
But whilst many scenes delight, the end resuly doesn’t’ deliver a strong or engaged narrative.
The show is packed with beautiful, familiar tunes, but over all, lacks energy and anything new to say.
Amara Okereke blossoms in the role of Eliza, from humble flower girl to debutante, Okereke’s performance is flawless and utterly captivating.
Indeed, the whole production and pacing is a little too elegant, gliding elegantly along like a swan you might admire on a nearby river, but never really making a splash.
I pitied the cast whose gallant efforts to make this antediluvian theatre production engaging deserved the most credit.

cn.t: Sher's sumptuous Broadway transfer wins praise for its lavish production and Amara Okereke's star-making turn as Eliza, though some critics find the old-fashioned staging lacks bite and fails to fully address the show's dated gender politics.
